paragraphs: This paper connects formal logical reasoning with computation in neural networks. Its target is constructive, intuitionistic modal reasoning, and its proposed representation uses ensembles of networks to encode theories in that logic. The central question is whether a logical program can be represented by a collection of networks that actually carries out its computation.

The authors establish a correspondence: for every intuitionistic modal program, there is a neural network ensemble that computes it. This is stronger than showing that a network resembles a reasoning procedure on selected examples. It provides a general representational result for the class of programs considered, together with a massively parallel computational model.

The learning connection comes from the fact that the constituent networks can be trained on examples using standard neural learning algorithms. The result therefore lays groundwork for combining explicit knowledge, logical reasoning, and learning within one architecture. The abstract presents that integration as a direction enabled by the model, rather than as an already demonstrated complete learning system.
neurips-2005-a-connectionist-model-for-c.tldr: Neural network ensembles can compute intuitionistic modal programs, providing a parallel foundation for combining logical reasoning with learning.

paragraphs: Detecting a deformable object means recognizing it even when its visible arrangement changes. This paper represents objects through graphical models organized as hierarchical trees. The root represents the complete object, while elements farther down the tree describe simpler features. This gives the detector a way to relate local image evidence to an overall object interpretation.

The detection algorithm passes simple messages both upward and downward through this hierarchy. Information can therefore move between the simpler features and the complete object representation. The compositional structure matters because detection is organized around relationships between levels, rather than treating the full object as an indivisible image pattern.

The authors demonstrate detection of cats, horses, and hands, including images containing background clutter and occlusion. They report processing times below one second for 320-by-240 images. These results support the usefulness of the proposed hierarchy in the demonstrated settings. The paper also contrasts its approach with dynamic programming and belief propagation, placing the message-passing procedure alongside established alternatives.
neurips-2005-a-hierarchical-compositiona.tldr: A hierarchy of object parts supports rapid detection of deformable objects, with demonstrations on cats, horses, and hands amid clutter and occlusion.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate the boundary between inputs where a function lies above a chosen threshold and inputs where it lies below. The goal is specifically to identify that separation. The authors develop an active learning algorithm that chooses which function queries to make, directing computation toward learning the threshold boundary.

Several query-selection methods are investigated. They use entropy, misclassification rate, variance, and combinations of these quantities to guide experiment selection. These criteria express different ways of deciding which observation would be useful for distinguishing the two regions. The paper examines their behavior across multiple datasets rather than presenting only a single selection rule.

The authors then apply the algorithms to construct simultaneously valid confidence intervals, at confidence level 1 − α, for seven cosmological parameters. In that parameter-estimation application, experiments show an order-of-magnitude reduction in required computation. The result illustrates how actively identifying a threshold boundary can make a substantive inference task cheaper, with the reported reduction tied to the application studied.
neurips-2005-active-learning-for-identif.tldr: Active selection of function queries learns threshold boundaries and reduces computation by an order of magnitude in a cosmological parameter-estimation application.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates a five-layer neuromorphic vision processor assembled from multiple chips. Its components communicate spike events asynchronously through address-event representation, or AER. The communication scheme provides the common interface through which separate processing components participate in a larger visual system.

The hardware includes a retina chip, two convolution chips, a two-dimensional winner-take-all chip, a delay-line chip, and a learning classifier chip. Additional circuit boards handle computer interfacing and address-space remapping. These supporting boards are part of the integration: the demonstration concerns a connected processing system, including the infrastructure needed to route events among its components.

The processor combines analog and digital computation and is designed to learn classifications of a moving object's trajectories. That task links visual input with processing across time and an eventual learned decision. The authors present a complete experimental setup and measurement results. The contribution is therefore a concrete demonstration of multiple neuromorphic building blocks operating together, supporting the construction of layered vision hardware.
neurips-2005-aer-building-blocks-for-mul.tldr: A five-layer neuromorphic vision system connects specialized chips through asynchronous spike events to support learning moving-object trajectory classes.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analog focal-plane processor for directional edge filtering. The processor contains a 128-by-128 photodiode array, combining image sensing with the hardware used for visual preprocessing. Its task is to apply a small convolution kernel across the image so that edges with directional structure can be extracted.

The design performs a 4-by-4-pixel kernel convolution over all pixels in 256 simple analog processing steps. Its implementation combines cyclic access to image lines with row-parallel processing. These mechanisms work within an architecture that connects only nearest neighbors, allowing the required image-wide operation to be organized using local interconnections.

The authors fabricate a proof-of-concept CMOS chip and experimentally demonstrate edge filtering at 200 frames per second. This establishes that the processing arrangement was realized in working hardware. The significance lies in coordinating access and parallel computation so that a local-interconnect architecture can carry out directional filtering across an entire sensor array with a simple implementation.
neurips-2005-an-analog-visual-pre-proces.tldr: An analog image processor uses cyclic line access and local interconnections to demonstrate directional edge filtering at 200 frames per second.

paragraphs: Probabilistic explanations of visual perception often assume that the observer already has a generative model with the right structure. This paper asks how such structure could be acquired through experience. It shifts attention from using a model to interpret uncertain visual input toward learning which model can explain that input.

The authors argue that Bayesian model selection offers an appropriate account of this process, including the acquisition of more complex structures. Their experiments find that people learn subtle statistical properties of visual scenes without supervision. This makes the learning question relevant to behavior: the observers acquire information about scene statistics without being explicitly taught those properties.

The experimental findings are well captured by Bayesian model learning within a class of models that explain observed variables through independent hidden causes. The result supports this particular account of how perceptual models can be learned from experience. It connects unsupervised visual learning with probabilistic structure discovery, extending the explanatory role of Bayesian inference beyond decisions made with a predetermined model.
neurips-2005-bayesian-model-learning-in-.tldr: Experiments on unsupervised visual learning are well explained by Bayesian learning of models built from independent hidden causes.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional human motion from a single video view is ambiguous: similar silhouettes can correspond to several different poses. This paper develops a conditional probabilistic framework that explicitly accommodates multiple plausible hidden states. Its observations are descriptors of image silhouettes, and its predictions are linked over time.

The method, called kBME, combines kernel principal component analysis with a Conditional Bayesian Mixture of Experts. The first component creates low-dimensional nonlinear representations; the second learns predictors that can associate one observation with multiple possible states. Restricting inference to these spaces targets computational efficiency, motivated by strong nonlinear correlations in visual observations and hidden motion variables.

A conditional graphical model combines the predictors across time and propagates uncertainty. Empirical comparisons favor the approach over the tested regression, Kernel Dependency Estimation, and PCA-only techniques. It also produces results competitive with high-dimensional mixture predictors at a fraction of their computational cost. Demonstrations on real monocular videos show successful reconstruction of complex human motion, supporting the combination of compact representations and explicit ambiguity modeling.
neurips-2005-conditional-visual-tracking.tldr: A compact nonlinear probabilistic tracker reconstructs 3D human motion from monocular video while retaining multiple plausible poses and propagating uncertainty over time.

paragraphs: This paper examines algorithms for learning stochastic models of symbolic time series. The reference approach is a state-emitting hidden Markov model trained with the Baum–Welch algorithm. Against that familiar route, the authors review newer learning procedures based on observable operator models, or OOMs, for modeling similar kinds of sequence data.

Two of the procedures are versions of an efficiency-sharpening algorithm. They repeatedly improve the statistical efficiency of a sequence of OOM estimators, focusing on how effectively estimation uses the observations. Another procedure is a maximum-likelihood estimator for transition-emitting hidden Markov models, optimized through constrained gradient descent. The distinction between state-emitting and transition-emitting models is part of the comparison.

The paper brings these algorithms together and compares them with state-emitting HMM learning through expectation-maximization on synthetic and real data. Its contribution is an overview and empirical comparison of alternative estimation strategies for symbolic sequences. The abstract identifies the algorithms and evaluation settings without declaring one method a universal winner, so the findings should be understood as comparative evidence within the studied tasks.
neurips-2005-efficient-estimation-of-oom.tldr: The paper reviews OOM-based sequence-learning algorithms and compares them with conventional hidden Markov model training on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: This paper estimates intrinsic dimensionality through quantization: representing a distribution using a limited collection of representative values and measuring the resulting error. The relevant dimension is that of the manifold supporting the distribution. The authors use a relationship between this dimension and the asymptotic behavior of the best achievable quantization error.

That relationship is expressed through quantization dimension. Rather than leading to just one estimator, its definition produces a family of dimensionality-estimation algorithms. A limiting case coincides with an existing method based on packing numbers. This connection places the new approach and the packing-based method within a shared mathematical framework.

The analysis uses high-rate vector quantization to examine statistical consistency and behavior in the presence of noise. These questions concern whether estimates settle toward the intended dimension and how noisy observations affect the scheme. The contribution is therefore both an estimation approach and a framework for studying its statistical behavior, with the abstract describing analysis of these issues rather than an unconditional guarantee of accurate dimensionality recovery.
neurips-2005-estimation-of-intrinsic-dim.tldr: Quantization error provides a family of intrinsic-dimension estimators, connecting to packing-based estimation and enabling analysis of consistency and noise.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of Gaussian process regression as the training dataset grows. With n training examples, the abstract describes training as requiring roughly cubic computation and each prediction as requiring linear computation. These two costs create separate obstacles: building the model becomes expensive, and using it continues to depend on the size of the training set.

The authors introduce an approximation method based on kd-trees. The method targets both stages of computation, reducing the time spent training as well as the time spent making predictions. Its central contribution is thus a computational approach for making Gaussian process regression more practical on large datasets.

The reported finding is a significant reduction in both training and prediction time. This matters because accelerating only model fitting would leave the cost of repeated predictions in place, while accelerating only predictions would leave the initial training bottleneck. By addressing both, the proposed approximation tackles the two scaling problems identified in the paper's motivation.
neurips-2005-fast-gaussian-process-regre.tldr: A kd-tree-based approximation significantly reduces both training and prediction time for Gaussian process regression.

paragraphs: Many learning methods organize their computations around similarities between data points. This paper addresses numerical computation shared by kernel methods, spectral techniques, and Gaussian processes. Its focus is on the computational machinery underlying these approaches, offering a strategy that can apply across several learning domains.

The proposed strategy combines Krylov subspace iteration with fast N-body learning methods. These are brought together as a general solution approach for the numerical problems arising in similarity-based learning. The scope matters: the paper treats computational efficiency as a common challenge across methods, rather than tying its contribution to one prediction task or one type of dataset.

Experiments on datasets used for image segmentation, object detection, and dimensionality reduction show significant improvements in computation and storage. The paper also supplies theoretical bounds on numerical stability. Together, these contributions address resource use and the reliability of the numerical procedures. The experimental gains establish benefits in the tested settings, while the stability analysis provides a separate theoretical basis for assessing the methods.
neurips-2005-fast-krylov-methods-for-n-b.tldr: Combining Krylov iteration with fast N-body methods yields reported computation and storage gains for similarity-based learning, alongside theoretical stability bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to bound the generalization error of binary classifiers when their training examples may depend on one another. It considers a particular source of dependence: the training data are generated deterministically from an underlying sample of independent examples. Independence therefore remains present at the source, even though it need not hold among the derived training items.

The authors propose a general framework for analyzing this situation and derive generalization bounds for binary classification. Such bounds concern how training with the available observations relates to performance beyond them. The framework makes the construction of the dependent data part of the analysis, rather than assuming those derived examples are themselves independent.

The results also cover some ranking problems and clarify their relationship with binary classification. This extends the usefulness of the framework while preserving its stated scope: it addresses dependence produced through deterministic transformations of an independent sample. The contribution is a theoretical way to reason about these linked observations and learning tasks, rather than a claim covering every possible form of dependent data.
neurips-2005-generalization-error-bounds.tldr: A theoretical framework bounds classification and some ranking errors when dependent training data are deterministically derived from independent examples.

paragraphs: Detecting motion involves deciding which observations correspond to one another across time. This paper derives a Bayesian Ideal Observer that addresses motion detection and this correspondence problem together. The authors also obtain the classic Barlow and Tripathy model as an approximation, connecting their formulation to an established account.

Psychophysical experiments show that human performance follows trends similar to those of the ideal observer, but its overall level is much worse. The authors test whether degrading the ideal observer can explain this gap. Even the extreme degradations they investigate do not bring its performance close to the human results.

They therefore propose that people use general-purpose models of motion rather than the task-specific ideal strategy. Further experiments are consistent with a Slow-and-Smooth model and rule out the alternative Slowness model considered. The evidence favors an explanation involving the structure of the motion model people use, while consistency with Slow-and-Smooth remains support for that account rather than proof that it uniquely describes human motion perception.
neurips-2005-ideal-observers-for-detecti.tldr: Human motion-detection results favor a general-purpose Slow-and-Smooth model over the tested degraded ideal observers and a Slowness-only alternative.

paragraphs: A visual boundary can be conveyed by different cues, including luminance, texture, contrast, and motion. Some neurons respond similarly to the structure of that boundary regardless of which cue reveals it. This paper asks whether such cue-invariant responses can be learned from natural images rather than supplied as predefined response properties.

The authors extend a conceptual model of cue invariance so that it can describe both simple-type and complex-type cell responses. Using this model, they show that cue-invariant properties can emerge through unsupervised learning from natural image data. The result links these response properties to statistical structure in the visual input.

This expands the reach of statistical models of vision beyond more elementary neuronal responses. It also demonstrates learning feature detectors that go beyond detecting changes in average luminance. The work consequently provides a basis for more sophisticated data-driven image processing and computer vision methods. Those applications are presented as possibilities opened by the learned representations, while the demonstrated result concerns cue-invariant responses acquired from natural images.
neurips-2005-learning-cue-invariant-visu.tldr: Unsupervised learning from natural images produces simple- and complex-type visual responses that remain similar across different cues to scene structure.

paragraphs: A collection of prototype points can summarize a larger dataset, but the prototypes alone do not specify how they should be connected. This paper asks how to build a graph whose topology reflects the structure of the original points. The objective is to represent relationships through graph connections as well as through representative locations.

The authors propose a generative model based on the Delaunay graph of the prototypes. They use the expectation-maximization algorithm to learn the model's parameters. This places the graph representation within a statistical modeling framework, connecting the desired topology to a model of the observed point set.

The paper presents the approach as an initial step toward statistically grounded topological modeling. Its significance is the formulation of graph construction as a learning problem with a generative model and parameter-estimation procedure. The stated contribution is foundational: it develops a way to approach the relationship between prototypes, their connections, and the points they represent, rather than claiming a complete solution to topological learning.
neurips-2005-learning-topology-with-the-.tldr: A generative model built on a Delaunay graph uses expectation-maximization to take an initial step toward statistically learning point-set topology.

paragraphs: An image contour may mark the boundary of an occluding surface or represent a thin object such as a wire. Similar ambiguities arise in diagrams, where lines can be connectors or dividers. This paper develops representations and logic for assigning these interpretations to contrast edges and ridges in both natural and graphical scenes.

The approach encodes constraints among local image events, including edges, ridges, junctions, and alignments. It uses a sparse, heterogeneous Markov random field containing interpretation nodes and energy functions that express relationships between them. Loopy belief propagation is used to find a minimum-energy configuration representing a coordinated interpretation of the scene.

Across a range of prototypical examples, the resulting configurations agree with preferred human interpretations. These examples include illusory contours such as the Kanizsa Triangle and more difficult cases. The method also correctly interprets ambiguous hand-drawn box-and-connector diagrams at low computational cost. The results show how local visual constraints can support coherent contour labeling in the examples studied.
neurips-2005-logic-and-mrf-circuitry-for.tldr: A Markov random field encodes contour relationships to interpret occlusion and thin lines, matching human preferences in studied examples and resolving ambiguous diagrams.

paragraphs: This paper develops estimation methods for Gaussian Markov processes that favor smoothness while still permitting discontinuities. These requirements must coexist: neighboring hidden quantities should generally vary smoothly, but some graph connections must allow abrupt changes. The authors investigate how weakening edges changes the posterior distribution over hidden nodes.

Their analysis considers that distribution as a whole rather than propagating information laterally between neighboring nodes. The resulting computation takes the form of feed-forward operations that collect multiple inputs, resembling the computational organization of V1 neurons. This provides an alternative way to organize inference when the model's smoothness relationships are perturbed.

The method also encounters matrix inverses and determinants. With suitable matrix preconditioners, the authors show that these quantities can be approximated without iteration using the same computational style. Simulations illustrate the approach's merits. The contribution is a route to non-iterative approximation and estimation that accommodates broken smoothness connections, with the matrix-approximation result specifically depending on appropriate preconditioning.
neurips-2005-non-iterative-estimation-wi.tldr: Analyzing graph-edge perturbations enables feed-forward estimation with smoothness and discontinuities, including non-iterative matrix approximations under suitable preconditioning.

paragraphs: Brain–computer interfaces translate brain activity into output without relying on the usual nerve and muscle pathways. This creates a possible communication and control route for people with paralysis. The paper focuses on a central technical requirement: distinguishing individual trials of brain signals accurately enough to support such an interface.

The proposed algorithm jointly optimizes spatial and spectral filters for multichannel EEG. The spatial component concerns how signals across channels are combined, while the spectral component concerns their frequency content. Optimizing them together aims to make the single-trial signals easier to distinguish for classification.

An evaluation covering 60 experiments and 22 subjects reports superior performance for the proposed algorithm. The benefit also extends to interpretation of the recorded signals: the learned spatial or spectral filters can support further analysis, including localization of sources associated with brain rhythms. The contribution therefore combines improved classification in the reported evaluation with filters that remain useful for examining the activity behind those decisions.
neurips-2005-optimizing-spatio-temporal-.tldr: Joint optimization of spatial and spectral EEG filters improves single-trial classification in an evaluation spanning 60 experiments and 22 subjects.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a probabilistic model for the statistical structure of images after a wavelet transform. The motivation is that understanding image statistics can support applications such as compression and restoration. The representation being modeled is therefore the transformed image, and the contribution concerns how its structure is described probabilistically.

The authors call their model a product of edge-perts. Alongside the modeling proposal, they develop a practical denoising algorithm based on a single edge-pert. This distinction matters: the broader probabilistic model and the demonstrated restoration procedure are related, but the denoising result is specifically attributed to a single component.

On benchmark images, the algorithm achieves what the authors report as state-of-the-art denoising performance. This supplies an application-based demonstration of the usefulness of their image model. Although compression is part of the motivation for studying image statistics, the stated experimental finding concerns denoising. The paper thus links a proposed statistical representation to a concrete image-restoration method and reported benchmark results.
neurips-2005-products-of-edge-perts-ce79.tldr: A probabilistic model of wavelet-transformed images leads to a single-edge-pert denoiser with reported state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks nonlinear representations of high-dimensional data. Sparsity can mean reducing the number of dimensions, but it can also mean representing the data through a selected subset of observations. This paper focuses on that second form: choosing landmark points that can support a compact manifold model.

The proposed algorithm selects landmarks using LASSO regression. Its l1 regularization encourages sparse approximations, making it suitable for choosing a subset rather than relying on every observation. Landmark selection addresses a computational concern because many manifold-learning methods have costs that grow quadratically with the number of observations.

The procedure also produces a continuous parameterization of the manifold based on the selected landmarks. It therefore supplies both representative points and a way to describe the manifold through them. Experiments on synthetic and real data illustrate the algorithm. The contribution connects a sparsity-promoting regression method with manifold representation, addressing the desire for compact models motivated by computational cost and generalization.
neurips-2005-selecting-landmark-points-f.tldr: LASSO-based landmark selection builds sparse manifold representations and also yields a continuous parameterization from the chosen points.

paragraphs: Winner-take-all networks perform a competitive computation that selects a winner among inputs. This paper studies that computation in a network of integrate-and-fire neurons receiving actual spike trains. The distinction matters because earlier studies, including some using spiking neurons, considered analog input rates rather than individual incoming spikes.

The authors show how to configure network connectivity so that a winner is selected after a predetermined number of input spikes. This links the decision process to the arrival of discrete events. They discuss both regularly timed inputs and inputs with Poisson-distributed rates, considering different forms of spike-train input within the same computational setting.

To test robustness, the network is implemented on an analog VLSI array containing 64 integrate-and-fire neurons. Those neurons have inherent variation in their operating parameters, so the hardware test exposes the computation to physical differences among units. The paper combines a connectivity-based account of spike-driven selection with an implementation used to examine robustness under that device variability.
neurips-2005-spiking-inputs-to-a-winner-.tldr: An integrate-and-fire winner-take-all network can be configured to select a winner after a predetermined number of incoming spikes.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a theoretical question about kernel canonical correlation analysis: whether functions estimated from a finite sample approach the true functions as more data become available. The method had already been applied to many problems, but the abstract identifies this asymptotic convergence question as an unresolved part of its statistical foundation.

The authors provide a rigorous convergence proof for kernel CCA and for a related method called NOCCO. This gives theoretical support for the estimation procedures by connecting what they learn from samples with their underlying target functions. The contribution concerns statistical convergence, rather than simply whether a numerical optimization procedure finishes.

The analysis also gives a sufficient condition governing how the regularization coefficient decreases as the sample grows. Following that condition ensures convergence within the result's scope. A sufficient condition supplies a valid route to the guarantee; it does not establish that every other schedule must fail. The paper therefore contributes both a foundational proof and guidance about regularization in the asymptotic setting.
neurips-2005-statistical-convergence-of-.tldr: The paper proves statistical convergence of kernel CCA and NOCCO and gives a sufficient condition on regularization decay.

paragraphs: This paper argues that many learning algorithms are limited by the variability of the function they seek to learn. It considers methods that rely solely on smoothness assumptions and express similarity through local kernels. Their predictions depend chiefly on nearby training examples, making them vulnerable to a form of the curse of dimensionality.

For Gaussian kernels, the authors show that learning a function with many variations requires a number of training examples proportional to those variations. A function can nevertheless have a short overall description, or low Kolmogorov complexity. Local variation can therefore make learning expensive even when the underlying structure is compact.

The discussion spans supervised, semisupervised, and unsupervised learning. Its implication is that exploiting broader structure could matter more than simply assuming nearby examples behave similarly. The authors suggest that nonlocal algorithms may learn such structured functions without highly specific domain knowledge. This is a statement of potential, while the concrete theoretical result identifies a sample requirement for the Gaussian-kernel setting.
neurips-2005-the-curse-of-highly-variabl.tldr: Local Gaussian-kernel learners can require samples proportional to target variations even when the function has a compact underlying description.

paragraphs: This paper models the intervals between neuronal spikes with a gamma distribution. The model separates a time-dependent firing rate from a shape parameter describing irregularity. The estimation problem is difficult because the firing rate changes with the environment and its time dependence is an unknown function.

The authors aim to estimate the irregularity parameter without first estimating that entire function. They use estimating functions from information geometry and analytically derive an optimal estimating function for the shape parameter. Its form does not depend on the functional form of the changing firing rate, addressing the nuisance function within this semiparametric model.

The abstract reports efficient estimation without loss of Fisher information and an advantage over maximum-likelihood estimation. These claims concern the gamma interspike-interval model under study. The significance is that a changing activity level need not be reconstructed explicitly to estimate the parameter of interest. The method offers a mathematically derived way to characterize spiking irregularity while leaving the unknown firing-rate function unestimated.
neurips-2005-unbiased-estimator-of-shape.tldr: An information-geometric estimator measures spiking irregularity in a gamma interval model without estimating the unknown time-varying firing rate.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a compact probabilistic representation of genetic diversity called an epitome. It consists of one short sequence, or a small collection of short sequences, of probability distributions. The representation captures many overlapping subsequences from a larger dataset, adapting an idea previously used for images and audio to discrete genetic sequences.

The model targets genetic applications including alignment and inference about recombination and mutation. The experiments focus on HIV diversity and the design of relatively small vaccine sequences covering many immune targets, called epitopes. Compact representation matters here because the aim is to include broad target coverage within a limited sequence length.

In the experiments, epitome designs contain more epitopes than similarly sized designs based on consensus-strain cocktails, phylogenetic tree centers, or observed strains. The authors also consider uncertainty in T-cell cross-reactivity and epitope presentation, finding the optimization fairly robust to those uncertainties. These results support the sequence-design approach through target coverage and optimization behavior; they are not a demonstration of protective vaccine efficacy.
neurips-2005-using-epitomes-to-model-gen.tldr: Compact genetic epitomes cover more HIV immune targets than the tested vaccine designs of similar length and show fairly robust optimization under modeled uncertainties.
